title: 1 Samuel 6:10–18
context: The men do as they were told. They take two milk cows, tie them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home. They set the LORD’s ark on the cart, with the box of golden mice and images of tumors. The cows take the straight way by the way to Beth Shemesh, go along the highway, lowing as they go, and do not turn to the right hand or to the left; the Philistine lords follow them to the border. The people of Beth Shemesh are reaping the wheat harvest in the valley; they lift up their eyes, see the ark, and rejoice. The cart comes into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stands there, where there is a great stone. They split the wood of the cart and offer the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD. The Levites take down the ark and the box and set them on the great stone, and the men of Beth Shemesh offer burnt offerings and sacrifices that day. When the five lords have seen it, they return to Ekron. The golden tumors are listed for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, one each, and the golden mice according to all the cities of the five lords, even to the great stone, which remains to this day in that field. Both traditions read the cows’ straight path as the LORD’s providence, answering the test of verse 9 without turning that test into an approved method. The joy, the offerings, and the stone are Israel’s first response to the ark’s return; the next unit will show that joy is not yet the same as holy fear.

verses.text: The men did so, and took two milk cows and tied them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men did so, and took two milk cows and tied them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home. The plan of verses 7–9 is actually carried out.

Arminian readers hear a real following-through. They do what their priests advised: the cows are yoked, the calves are kept back, and the test is now in motion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the Philistines’ obedience to their own counsel. The calves are shut up at home, so the next verse’s journey will run against a mother’s pull.

Both traditions read the verse as the setup being put into action, shared narrative ground for the path that follows.

verses.text: They put the LORD’s ark on the cart, and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors.
verses.arminianNotes:
They put the LORD’s ark on the cart, and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors. The holy ark and the pagan offering now travel together, the gold in a box at its side.

Arminian readers hear the arrangement exactly as planned. The ark is no longer held in Philistine houses; it is set on the cart to go, with the jewels of the trespass offering beside it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that it is still “the LORD’s ark” that they lay on the cart. The box of images goes with it as their offering, not as a rival object of the same honor.

Both traditions take the loading of the cart as the last Philistine act before the cows move, on shared ground.

verses.text: The cows took the straight way by the way to Beth Shemesh. They went along the highway, lowing as they went, and didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left; and the lords of the Philistines went after them to the border of Beth Shemesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The cows took the straight way by the way to Beth Shemesh.” They went along the highway, lowing as they went, “and didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left”; the lords of the Philistines went after them to the border of Beth Shemesh.

Arminian readers hear providence in a straight path, and they hear it all the more because the cows are lowing. Their instinct is toward the calves; they still do not turn aside. The sign the Philistines asked for is given, and it is the LORD who takes the ark home, without that fact turning their test into a method Israel is taught to use.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same overruling. The cows take the straight way, keep to the highway, and do not turn right or left, while the lords walk after them as witnesses to the border. The lowing shows that the journey is costly for the animals; the direction is not explained by ease or training.

Both traditions take the verse as the LORD’s answer in the event, shared ground: this is his hand, not chance, and not an endorsement of divination.

verses.text: The people of Beth Shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley; and they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, and rejoiced to see it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people of Beth Shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley; and they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, and rejoiced to see it. The scene is set at wheat harvest, and the first response is joy.

Arminian readers hear a real gladness. The ark, long gone in Philistine country, is seen again, and they rejoice to see it. Joy here is right, even if verse 19 will show that gladness must still be joined to reverence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the harvest notice and the lifted eyes as the narrator’s way of placing the return in ordinary work. They see the ark and rejoice; the following verses will add offering, and then judgment.

Both traditions read the verse as joyful recognition of the ark’s return, shared ground in the valley of Beth Shemesh.

verses.text: The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, and stood there, where there was a great stone. Then they split the wood of the cart and offered up the cows for a burnt offering to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, and stood there, where there was a great stone. Then they split the wood of the cart and offered up the cows for a burnt offering to the LORD.

Arminian readers hear the cart stopping at a named field and a great stone, and a first act of worship. Joshua of Beth Shemesh is the owner of the field, not Joshua son of Nun. The cows and the cart’s wood become a burnt offering to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the cart “stood there” at the great stone, and that the offering is made to the LORD. The journey ends where they can worship; the stone will be named again in verses 15 and 18.

Both traditions take the stop and the burnt offering as Israel’s first corporate response, shared ground, without a dispute over the use of the cart as fuel.

verses.text: The Levites took down the LORD’s ark and the box that was with it, in which the jewels of gold were, and put them on the great stone; and the men of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices the same day to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites took down the LORD’s ark and the box that was with it, in which the jewels of gold were, and put them on the great stone; and the men of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices the same day to the LORD.

Arminian readers hear a right care for the ark. Levites handle it and the box, and set them on the stone; the people add burnt offerings and sacrifices the same day. The ark is not left as a spectacle in the field.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that Levites take the ark down, a priestly handling in a sudden scene, and that the offerings are made to the LORD that same day. The gold remains in its box, now on the stone beside the ark.

Both traditions take the verse as worship and as the Levites’ careful handling of the ark, which makes the irreverence reported in verse 19 stand out all the more, without yet stating that judgment.

verses.text: When the five lords of the Philistines had seen it, they returned to Ekron the same day.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the five lords of the Philistines had seen it, they returned to Ekron the same day. The witnesses of the test have seen enough, and they go home.

Arminian readers hear the sign completed for those who proposed it. They followed the cart to the border; they see the reception at Beth Shemesh; they return to Ekron the same day, their question of verse 9 answered in the event.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the five lords see it and return. The path to Beth Shemesh was not a private Israelite claim; Philistine rulers were present for the ending as for the sending.

Both traditions read the verse as the close of the Philistine testimony, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned for a trespass offering to the LORD: for Ashdod one, for Gaza one, for Ashkelon one, for Gath one, for Ekron one;
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned for a trespass offering to the LORD: for Ashdod one, for Gaza one, for Ashkelon one, for Gath one, for Ekron one. The five cities are named, one image each; the sentence runs on into the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a city-by-city catalogue of the offering already described. The names are the Philistine pentapolis, written as the WEB spells them, and the tumors are returned to the LORD, not kept as charms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the list as the narrator’s inventory of that trespass offering: five tumors for the five lords’ cities, to the LORD. The offering remains what they made; it is now recorded as having been returned.

Both traditions read the verse as a factual list, without a contrast over the geography of the five cities.

verses.text: and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both of fortified cities and of country villages, even to the great stone on which they set down the LORD’s ark. That stone remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
The catalogue continues with the golden mice, “according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both of fortified cities and of country villages,” even to the great stone on which they set down the LORD’s ark. “That stone remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.”

Arminian readers hear a memorial left in the field. The stone is still there in the narrator’s day; it marks where the ark was set down. How the number of mice here relates to the five of verse 4 is a detail some readers notice; it need not be forced into a contradiction or a settled scheme.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same stone, “to this day”, in Joshua of Beth Shemesh’s field, as the narrator’s closing witness to the return. The mice are counted by all the cities, fortified and villages, belonging to the five lords.

Both traditions take the verse as the end of the offering list and as a lasting marker of the event, shared ground, without a debate over the later fate of the stone.
